Marathon Petroleum's stock has fallen 2% over five trading days, closing at $457.22 today, despite sitting near the middle of that decline. The underlying reason appears counterintuitive: while oil prices have climbed sharply—Brent crude hit $116 and U.S. crude sits at nearly $108—refiners like Marathon face a headwind. Refineries are running at 93.4% capacity, and gasoline and diesel inventories are elevated (205 and 104 million barrels respectively), which means refining margins are being squeezed. Higher crude prices flow into refined products more slowly when storage is already full, eating into profit per barrel processed.

The broader pattern reflects a tension in energy markets: geopolitical risk is pushing crude prices up, but the refining industry hasn't yet benefited because demand hasn't caught up with supply. Refineries can't run much hotter than 93%, and full storage tanks mean they can't convert higher-priced crude into profits as efficiently as they could in tighter inventory conditions.
